beats.narration: Begin by framing Pipeline Foundation: Vertex Processing as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. The OpenGL graphics pipeline processes vertices through programmable shader stages. Consider this worked case: Vertex attributes like position and normal are passed from the application to the vertex shader for initial transformation. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Pipeline Foundation: Vertex Processing
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a flowchart showing vertices entering the vertex shader stage with labeled input/output attributes.

beats.narration: Now define Primitive Assembly precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. Primitive assembly groups vertices into points, lines, or triangles. Consider this worked case: Three consecutive vertex indices are connected to form a triangle primitive that defines a planar surface. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Primitive Assembly
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a wireframe triangle with numbered vertex indices and a line connecting them to a primitive assembly buffer.

beats.narration: With the foundation in place, examine how View Volume Clipping operates in a concrete sequence. Clipping removes portions outside the view volume. Consider this worked case: A triangle extending beyond the camera's frustum is clipped at the clipping plane boundaries. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: View Volume Clipping
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Illustrate a 3D cube with a frustum overlay, highlighting clipped edges and the resulting clipped polygon.

beats.narration: Next, compare the choices involved in Rasterization Conversion and make the decision criteria explicit. Rasterization converts primitives into fragment candidates. Consider this worked case: Each triangle is subdivided into a set of pixels, generating a fragment for every covered pixel. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis. Then summarize what the example demonstrates, what it does not establish, and what evidence would be needed next.
beats.title: Rasterization Conversion
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a subdivided triangle with a rasterization mask indicating which pixels are covered.

beats.narration: Apply Interpolation Values to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Interpolation produces per-fragment values from vertex outputs. Consider this worked case: Color and normal values are linearly interpolated across the triangle to determine per-fragment properties. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Interpolation Values
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a triangle with gradient shading showing interpolated color values moving from vertex to fragment.

beats.narration: Examine the tradeoffs in Fragment Processing, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. Fragment processing computes values for framebuffer operations. Consider this worked case: The fragment shader calculates final color, alpha, and depth values for each pixel. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Fragment Processing
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a fragment shader code snippet with labeled inputs and outputs mapping to framebuffer writes.

beats.narration: Stress-test the reasoning around Depth Testing Visibility with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Depth testing resolves visibility according to stored depth values. Consider this worked case: A fragment is discarded if its computed depth exceeds the stored depth value in the depth buffer. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.
beats.title: Depth Testing Visibility
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Illustrate a depth buffer comparison with a foreground fragment passing and a background fragment failing.

beats.narration: Use Blending Operations to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Blending combines a fragment result with an existing framebuffer value. Consider this worked case: Alpha blending mixes the new fragment color with the existing pixel color using a specified blend factor. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.
beats.title: Blending Operations
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a split screen with a semi-transparent overlay blending onto a base image using a blend equation.

beats.narration: Connect Coordinate Spaces and Sampling to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. Coordinate spaces, sampling, and numerical precision must remain explicit. Consider this worked case: Texture coordinates are explicitly mapped from object space to UV space to avoid sampling artifacts. Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Coordinate Spaces and Sampling
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a texture coordinate grid on a 3D surface with explicit UV mapping lines and sampling points.

beats.narration: Finish with Practical Analysis Checklist as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. Visual correctness follows from explicit conventions, assumptions, sampling decisions, and measurable error. Consider this worked case: A checklist verifies explicit coordinate mappings, proper sampling rates, and error bounds before rendering. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a checklist graphic with checkboxes for explicit conventions, sampling decisions, measurable error, and assumptions.

sources.excerpt: Computer graphics uses geometric models to represent objects and scenes. Transformations position and orient geometry within coordinate systems. Viewing maps a scene through a camera model to an image. Rasterization samples projected primitives on a discrete pixel grid. Shading models how light, material, and geometry determine appearance. Texture mapping associates image data with geometric surfaces. Curves and surfaces provide compact smooth shape representations. Animation changes scene state over time. Ray tracing follows visibility and light paths through a scene. Visual correctness follows from explicit conventions, assumptions, sampling decisions, and measurable error.
